text: CI/CD culture wants to move fast: frequent, small, low-risk deployments, shipped as soon as they pass their pipeline. Traditional Change Enablement, which Course 8 built out in depth, wants the opposite instinct applied first: careful review, documented risk, and sign-off from people who understand the blast radius of what's changing. Neither side is wrong. A pipeline shipping ten small, well-tested fixes a day genuinely reduces risk compared to one enormous, rarely-tested release. And a CAB insisting on reviewing a change to core approval logic for a business-critical process is also genuinely protecting the organization. The tension is real, not manufactured.

Blanket fast-tracking — treating every pipeline deployment as automatically approved — throws away exactly what Change Enablement exists to catch: the rare change that's small in code but large in business consequence. Blanket gatekeeping — routing every pipeline-driven change through full CAB review — throws away exactly what CI/CD exists to deliver: shipping routine, low-risk fixes without a multi-day approval cycle. Mature implementations do neither. They differentiate by risk.

The mechanism that makes this work is one Course 8 already taught: the Standard Change template, a pre-approved category for well-understood, low-risk, repeatable work. A change backed by strong ATF coverage from Chapter 4 — UI tests, server-side tests, and scheduled suite runs all passing — has real, automated evidence of low risk. That evidence is exactly what justifies routing its deployment through a pre-approved Standard Change template: fast, low-friction, and still a real, governed Change Request.

A change that's genuinely risky — touching core approval logic, security configuration, or anything with wide business impact — still warrants full CAB review, even if its automated tests pass. Passing tests prove the code does what the tests checked for. They don't by themselves prove the change is low-risk to the business. Test coverage and business risk are related, but they are not the same measurement.

This isn't splitting the difference between speed and control — it's using each tool for what it's actually good at. ATF and CI/CD generate real, continuous evidence about technical soundness; Change Enablement's risk classification uses that evidence to decide which changes deserve the fast path and which still need a human in the loop. Next: a worked lab applying exactly this decision to a real deployment scenario.
